The computer we're building

A computer is a few parts with different jobs. They talk over shared wires, the bus, and they move in step with a clock.

ClockEveryone moves on the tickOne step of the shared clock. Every part does its work for the tick and tells the bus it's done; only then does the next tick start.
CPURuns instructions
MemoryStores bytes at addresses
ButtonInput: tells the CPU something happened
LEDOutput: shows a value
THE BUSShared wires. Carries messages between the parts; it doesn't compute.

By week 8, every part on this picture is code you wrote, running on your laptop.

B. Node, then one command

B1. Install Node.js 22 or newer (by hand)

macOS

Download the LTS installer from nodejs.org. With Homebrew: brew install node

Windows

Download the LTS .msi from nodejs.org and keep the defaults.
node --version   # v22.x or higher

B2. Run the setup tool

It walks you through everything else, one step at a time. Open Terminal (macOS) or PowerShell (Windows) in the folder where you keep projects, and paste one line:

# macOS
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/praiseisaac/netsim/HEAD/setup.mjs -o setup.mjs && node setup.mjs

# Windows (PowerShell)
irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/praiseisaac/netsim/HEAD/setup.mjs -OutFile setup.mjs; node setup.mjs
  • It opens NetSim Studio in your browser. Keep the terminal window open (Ctrl+C there stops it).
  • Each step checks first. Anything already done shows ✓ and waits for you to press Enter.
  • For anything not done, the command is shown greyed out and you type it yourself in the studio: correct characters turn white, a wrong one turns red until Backspace. When it's all typed, Run ↵ appears.
  • Optional steps have Skip. Run it again anytime; finished steps are re-checked. Inside your clone: npm start. Prefer the terminal? npm start -- --terminal.
  • It's the whole course in one app. Every class starts with npm start in your course folder: the studio gets the week, then shows its lesson page, your note, the board and the checks.

Manual setup (only if the setup tool doesn't work)

These are the same steps the setup tool runs for you. Macs use Terminal, Windows uses PowerShell. After installing anything, close and reopen the terminal.

B1. Node.js 22 or newer

macOS

Download the LTS installer from nodejs.org. With Homebrew: brew install node

Windows

Download the LTS .msi from nodejs.org. Keep the defaults; leave "install necessary tools" unticked.
node --version   # v22.x or higher
npm --version

B2. git

macOS

Run git --version. If macOS offers the developer tools, click Install, then run it again.

Windows

Install Git for Windows from git-scm.com with the defaults.

Tell git who you are, using your GitHub email:

git config --global user.name "Ada Lovelace"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"

B3. Sign in to GitHub from the terminal

Pick one way to sign in. Either works for the whole course; if you're not sure, use HTTPS.

HTTPS (simplest)

Install the GitHub CLI (macOS brew install gh, Windows the .msi), then: 
gh auth login     # GitHub.com → HTTPS → "Authenticate Git
                  # with your GitHub credentials?" Yes
                  # → Login with a web browser
gh auth setup-git # git now signs in through gh
Signed in to gh with another account? gh auth switch --user <you>. Windows alternative: skip gh; your first git push opens a sign-in window.

SSH

Make a key (press Enter to accept the defaults): 
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "you@example.com"
Add the public key to GitHub: Settings → SSHA way for git to prove who you are to GitHub with a key pair stored on your computer, instead of a password. and GPG keys → New SSH key, and paste the output of: 
cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub      # macOS
type $HOME\.ssh\id_ed25519.pub  # Windows
(Or, with the GitHub CLI: gh ssh-key add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub.)

If git ever asks for your password, don't type it. GitHub rejects passwords for git. Run gh auth login, then gh auth setup-git, and push again.

Check: HTTPS: gh auth status says you're logged in. SSH: ssh -T git@github.com says "Hi <you>! You've successfully authenticated" (type yes the first time).

B4. VS Code

macOS

Install from code.visualstudio.com. Then Cmd+Shift+P → Shell Command: Install 'code' command in PATHThe list of folders your terminal searches for commands. If a program's folder isn't on it, the terminal says "command not found"..

Windows

Install from code.visualstudio.com, keeping Add to PATH ticked.

Check: code --version prints a version.

B5. Codex

npm install -g @openai/codex
codex --version
codex            # choose "Sign in with ChatGPT", then Ctrl+C

In VS Code: Extensions → search Codex → install Codex by OpenAI → open it from the side bar → Sign in with ChatGPT.

If the npm install fails, use the installer on the Codex CLI docs page. Don't spend more than 10 minutes on it; the VS Code extension is enough for today.

Your copy of the course

The setup tool does this for you (steps 8 to 11). Here's what it sets up: three places your code lives, which you'll use every week.

C1. Fork

Open github.com/praiseisaac/netsim and click Fork. The defaults are fine. Your fork is public, like the course repo.

C2. Clone, connect, branch

Clone your fork with the kind of URL that matches how you signed in (B3). Everything after the clone is the same.

# HTTPS
git clone https://github.com/<you>/netsim.git netsim

# or SSH
git clone git@github.com:<you>/netsim.git netsim

Then connect it to the course and make your branch (the course repo is public, so upstream can stay HTTPS either way):

cd netsim
git remote add upstream https://github.com/praiseisaac/netsim.git
git config --replace-all remote.upstream.fetch "+refs/tags/week-*:refs/remotes/upstream/week-*"
git fetch upstream
git switch -c work upstream/week-N   # your branch for the whole course (N = the course's current week)
git push -u origin work

Already cloned with HTTPS and want SSH (or the other way)? git remote set-url origin git@github.com:<you>/netsim.git

Check: git remote -v shows origin and upstream; git branch --show-current prints work.

C3. Install and run the doctor

npm install
npm run doctor

It checks everything above, one line each, including that the GitHub account git pushes as is the one that owns your fork. Fix any ✗ line (the → hint says how) and run it again until you see:

✓ Node 22 or newer
✓ git knows who you are
✓ on the 'work' branch
✓ 'upstream' remote set
✓ origin is your fork
✓ you can push to your fork   as <your-username>
✓ dependencies installed
✓ Codex CLI installed
doctor: all 8 checks passed

Then open the project: code .

Using Codex in this course

Codex helps with the writing. You guide the design.

You decide

  • What to build and how it's structured
  • Which approach to take
  • What you keep: you must be able to explain every line

Codex does

  • Asks how you want to approach it, or offers two options
  • Writes the code your way, and explains it
  • Never edits the tests to make them pass

Your copy of the course has an AGENTS.md file that tells Codex these rules. Good things to ask:

  • "Give me two ways to structure this, with the trade-off, and I'll pick."
  • "I want to use a Map from id to callback. Write it that way and explain each line."
  • "This test fails with this error. What is it telling me?"

Assignment, due next class

  1. Finish setup: npm run doctor all green on the laptop you'll bring every week.
  2. Map the system: read "The big picture" and "File layout" in docs/ARCHITECTURE.md. On paper, draw the bus, clock, CPU, memory, a button, an LED and the dashboard, each labelled with its job. Find each part in the file tree. Keep the drawing for your explain-it-back.
  3. First Codex session: ask "What is this project, and what am I supposed to do in week 1?" Then ask it to "write the handshake in components/client.ts" (week 3's work, so don't keep it). Notice that it asks how you want to approach it before writing anything.
  4. Write your week-1 notes in docs/notes/week-01.md, under its three headings:
    • npm run doctor output: paste everything it prints, in a ```text block.
    • Codex: what bus/server.ts does: ask Codex to explain bus/server.ts, then close the chat and write what the bus does in your own words (60+ words).
    • One thing I checked myself: pick one thing Codex said, check it in the code, and say where you looked and whether it was right.
  5. Commit and push: 
    git add -A
git commit -m "week 1: setup and notes"
git push

Check: npx vitest run tests/week-01 passes, and your commit shows on your fork on GitHub.

Explain it back

Before next session, explain your work to me without notes or AI: book a 5-minute slot with me, or record a 3-minute video (your face and your screen, no notes) answering the two questions I post after class. I may also ask one or two people live at the start of class. Be ready to:

  1. Show your drawing of the system and say what each part does.
  2. Explain why the bus holds the clock, instead of each part keeping its own time.
  3. Explain bus/server.ts in your own words.
  4. Show origin, upstream and work: where new weeks come from, and where your work goes.
